newsitem.title: USA: NJ governor to use tobacco money for charity care.
newsitem.headline: NJ governor to use tobacco money for charity care.

text.p: New Jersey Gov. Christine Whitman on Friday said she would use the state's share of a proposed settlement with the tobacco industry to finance charity health care.

Whitman, speaking at a press conference after an announcement of the proposed settlement in Washington, did not provide an estimate of how much the state expected to receive from the agreement, which would cost the industry $368.5 billion over 25 years.
Whitman said her administration would not rely on an early disbursement to pay for charity care in 1998.
"But in the future, it's an appropriate use of dollars from the settlement," she said.
New Jersey sued the tobacco industry for $50 billion, but will likely see no more than $9 billion or $10 billion over the next 25 years, an administration source said.

By law, New Jersey's acute care hospitals must treat all patients without regard to ability to pay. The very poor are covered by Medicaid, but upwards of one million New Jerseyans are not covered at work or are dependents of uncovered workers.

The care given these medical indigents is paid for by the state from a $300 million fund, diverted from a payroll tax that otherwise supports unemployment insurance. That system was the result a two-year compromise to allow the administration to find a more palatable and reliable means of supporting charity care, but is set to expire in December.
